record.original_question: Let X be a smooth acyclic surface with the property that for every nonconstant regular function p in C[X] there exists another regular function q in C[X] such that the morphism F=(p,q): X -> C^2 is proper. Must X be isomorphic to C^2?

evidence.quote: OUESTION. Let X be a smooth acyclic surface such that for any non–constant regular function p ∈ C[X] there exists another one q ∈ C[X] with the property that F = (p, q ) : X → C2 is a proper morphism. Is it true that X is isomorphic to C2 ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex algebraic surface that is acyclic, meaning that its reduced singular cohomology $\tilde H^*(X;\mathbb{Z})$ vanishes. Suppose $X$ has the following property: for every nonconstant regular function $p \in \mathbb{C}[X]$, there exists a regular function $q \in \mathbb{C}[X]$ such that the morphism
$$F = (p,q): X \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^2$$
is proper. Must $X$ be isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^2$ as an algebraic variety?
artifact.status_search_result: A brief web search did not return a definitive resolution of this characterization. There are partial characterizations of $\mathbb{C}^2$ among smooth acyclic surfaces (by Miyanishi–Sugie, Kaliman, Zaidenberg, and others) using the existence of suitable families of curves or $\mathbb{C}^*$-actions, but no source clearly resolves the specific properness-based criterion stated here. The status is therefore reported as unknown.

status_evidence.title: Isotrivial families of curves on affine surfaces and characterization of the affine plane
status_evidence.snippet: characterization of C2 as a smooth acyclic algebraic surface on which there exist simply connected algebraic curves ... or isotrivial families of curves with base C
status_evidence.claim: Related characterizations of C^2 among smooth acyclic surfaces exist, but use different criteria than properness of (p,q).

status_evidence.title: On Proper Polynomial Maps of C^2
status_evidence.snippet: On proper polynomial maps of C^2
status_evidence.claim: Literature on proper polynomial maps focuses on C^2 itself, not on settling this acyclic-surface question.
